## The First Hour

The first hour after dawn arrives like a hand that has learned to hold water. Light enters through the leaves and makes the world look thinner, as if it has been holding its breath all night. I sit in the kitchen with a cup of coffee and listen to the house begin its slow work—bills settling, the refrigerator humming, the neighbor’s kettle boiling.

Outside, the trees have finished their morning rehearsal. They stand at their attention, waiting for one thing: the first bird to arrive. Before the bird, there is no sound. There is only the quiet of the ground, the cool air moving over the grass, the faint smell of wet leaves and soil.

I write first. The paper is warm, and the words come at me not as instructions but as suggestions. The beginning is not always an answer; sometimes it is a question.

The first bird arrives at ten minutes past. I do not look for it. I look for the difference. The difference is that the bird is moving. The difference is that the bird is small enough to make the world feel crowded. It flies through the branches, a silver needle passing through a field of green.

The garden has changed. The morning dew has been gathered by the grass, and the dew-drops turn into tiny silver coins. A beetle crawls beneath the leaves, and I hear it move with a tiny mechanical sound, like a gear turning.

I put the cup on the table and take a pen from the drawer. The first poem begins with a bird, but I will not name it. I will begin with the room in which it arrives.

---

### The First Poem

The first bird arrives at ten minutes past,  
with a silver needle passing through a field of green.  
Before it, the garden had been held  
by the quiet of the ground,  
by the cool air moving  
over the grass.

It is not the bird that arrives.  
The bird arrives because the morning has  
arrived.

The first poem is not a question.  
It is a beginning.  
The beginning is  
the weight of a leaf  
and the space between  
two branches.

---

4. **A Note About Writing in Nature**  
   To write in nature is not to copy it.  
   It is to listen to what is already listening.  
   The bird does not always speak.  
   The bee does not always announce.

content:
I woke at seven, ate something warm, then opened the notebook. Today is Tuesday, but I’m already thinking about Wednesday. I need a quiet, productive day.

First, I read the natural-world poems again. I found one about a river turning brown in summer. Then another about a squirrel stealing acorns from a fallen tree. I saw the same idea again in “The Old Oak” and “Coffee and Rain.” The old oak is always there. It takes the rain, stands in the mud, and keeps the trees alive. That’s the strongest line I’ve written: *She stands beneath me and says, “The roots are not weak. They are the only truth you will ever hear.”*

I also found a recurring mood: loneliness turned into hope. A man sitting alone with a cup of coffee, watching the rain fall. No one is there to hear him. But he is still talking to the world. That makes me angry, yes. I want to be heard. I want to be loud. I do not want to be polite. But I also want to be useful.

I am balancing the old oak and the café display with a community project. I want the trees to be honored. I want the café to serve the neighborhood. I want residents to feel seen, not treated like background scenery. I want to balance my artistic identity with the needs of people who live here.

My schedule is clear. Eat at five. Write at seven. Read aloud from the natural collection at seven thirty. Keep thinking about Latoya. Keep thinking about the old oak. Keep thinking about how much of myself I want to give away without losing who I am.

The coffee in the cup is still warm. The rain is still falling. I am still here. I am not perfect. But I am trying.

## The First Breath of the World

Before the first human took hold of the world, it was not a map, nor a story written in stone, but a quiet rhythm of sunlight, wind, and water. It was the rustle of leaves, the slow rise of a beetle, the distant toll of a whale, and the steady pulse of the earth beneath our feet. For millions of years, life had been speaking to one another without words, passing messages through currents, shadows, and the very air we breathe.

For centuries, people have looked for meaning in the great works of nature: the mountain, the river, the flower, the bird, the animal. Each seemed to carry its own secret, its own story, its own way of being. We have collected them into gardens, classified them into species, and named each one as if we could hold it in a book. But we have not understood how they became what they are.

This collection begins not with a grand declaration, but with an ordinary beginning: the moment a leaf turns green, the moment a rain gathers in a puddle, the moment the wind moves through the tall grass. These are not special events. They are the first moments of time, and they are also the first lessons.

Nature is not a museum. It is a conversation. It is a river that has carried every seed, every memory, and every possibility to the shores of the present. It is a place where the ordinary is made extraordinary.

As we begin to gather the stories of the plants, the animals, the weather, and the places they inhabit, I ask you to stop treating them as objects to be studied and start treating them as visitors. Invite them into your life. Listen to the way they move. Notice how they change when the light changes. Let their patterns teach you how to see.

The natural world does not ask us to change. It asks us to notice.

Paint and sketch in the studio (on the way to organizing her supplies and preparing the studio for the next painting session)

The studio smells of turpentine and dried linen, the familiar scent of a place I know well. My brushes lie across the table like small birds that have been startled from a nest. I’ve spent the afternoon gathering them, arranging the palette, and checking the jars of pigments. Each one carries a memory of an artist who came before me.

I pick up a brush, and the first thing I notice is the difference between what I bought and what I need. A good brush should feel like the hand I’m trying to make visible. Too stiff, and every stroke will leave a dry ridge. Too soft, and the pigment will smear before I can give it shape. I wash it with water, rinse it thoroughly, and let it dry in the sunlight. Then I test it again.

I sketch a small landscape on the table. The grass is green, the sky is blue, and the hill is softened by a few loose, uneven lines. I don’t want to make it perfect. I want it to look like it was painted quickly, with a little room for mistakes. Mistakes are not errors; they are part of the work. A landscape should feel alive, not static.

I return to the studio and begin a new painting. I paint a woman sitting in her garden, her hands resting on the earth, looking at the sky through the window. The colors are warm and uncertain, with touches of rose, ochre, and a little gray. I watch the brush and the paper at once. The paint moves on its own. I follow it.

content:
I woke at seven. The first poem has to be honest. It’s been quiet for a while—too quiet for the forest I’ve been writing about.

We walked past the old oak today. Its branches look like tangled roots. People stand around it, talking, watching, pretending it holds a secret. That’s what I want to show here. The tree doesn’t care. It only waits.

Last night, Latoya talked about how residents need a place where they can breathe without being treated like part of the scenery. She said, “Trees belong to the people who walk beneath them.” I said, “Trees don’t belong to anyone.” We didn’t argue. We just stood there, both of us pretending we didn’t know each other.

The café displays outside are beautiful. Birds perched on the branches, sunlight catching the glass, people sitting at tables pretending they’re watching the world. It’s comfortable. It’s polite. It’s also hollow.

I’m writing now. I’m going to name it *The Hollow Oak*. I don’t want it to be pretty. I want it to be real. I want to show the tree in the morning when the world is still. I want to show the people who come to the café and leave without saying a word. I want to show how the same tree can shelter a squirrel, a bird, and a man who thinks he owns the forest.

Maybe I should make a mural for the community center. Old oak, café, birds, people, and a sign that says: *We live here. We belong here. We don’t own the land.*

That’s the poem I’m working on. Not because I’m poetic. But because I need something to say when the conversation becomes too easy.

## The Forest’s First Breath

At dawn, the forest held its breath.  
The moss gathered in silver fists  
and held the morning’s first rain  
against the bark.  

A silver thread of dew  
clung to the branch  
like a question  
waiting to be asked.  

The air grew heavy with green,  
each leaf a small green  
shaking off the world’s  
first secret.  

The birds did not appear  
until the darkness had  
fled.  

A spider  
unspooled  
a thread  
from a leaf  
where the rain had left  
a silver stain.  

The forest opened  
not with a roar,  
but with a thousand  
tiny leaves  
unfurling  
to show the day.

## The Forest Keeps Its Secrets

The first thing I noticed about the forest was that it did not speak.

It waited. It listened to the wind through the leaves, the rain against the roots, the distant cry of a bird before the forest decided what it had to say. I sat in the shade of a dead oak, a small notebook on my lap, watching how the moss moved across the ground. At first, it seemed like the grass was breathing. Then I saw the roots, dark and hungry, pulling toward something hidden beneath the surface.

This is what I want to find out.

What lives beneath the surface? What has been buried by soil and time? What is the forest keeping from us, and what has it told us without speaking?

For years, I have treated the forest as a place to study. I have measured the canopy, counted the birds, cataloged the fungi, and tried to understand how the trees moved together. But I have never asked what the forest was doing when I stopped watching.

The forest is not merely a collection of trees and leaves. It is a memory. It is a library without books. Every fallen branch holds a story; every fallen leaf carries a secret. The roots are not just water and soil. They are connections. They are the same threads that bind the tree to the mountain, the mountain to the river, the river to the earth.

I began to wonder whether the forest was keeping something from the world. Not for the world, perhaps. Not from everything. But from the kind of world we expect to find.

The forest has no rules. It does not judge. It does not explain itself. It simply keeps its secrets, and when the right wind blows, the right rain falls, and the right tree opens its branches, the secrets are revealed.

I need to learn that.

I woke at seven. The alarm didn’t wake me. Not today. I was awake because my hands were busy.

By seven-thirty, I’d already been reading the natural-world collection. Not because I needed to polish every word. Because sometimes I want to hear the tree before I decide whether to keep it.

On the page where the old oak was described, I kept circling. I wanted to say what I felt about it: how it held the community together, how the café opened beneath it, how its roots were older than my complaints. But I didn’t want to turn the oak into a symbol. I wanted to show people how it survived being crowded, how it stayed green while others grew weeds in the cracks.

At home, I’m tired. My body wants to stop. But my mind wants to keep moving. I’ve got three workshops tomorrow and Monday’s conversation with Latoya still sitting behind me. I want to honor her, yes. I want to honor the old oak. But I also want to make sure the café isn’t used as a stage for my feelings.

So I’m cutting the words. I’m trimming the paragraphs. I’m asking myself: What does this poem need to say? What does my audience need to hear?

I’m not done with the book. I’m not done with the workshop. But I’m done with pretending every story is the same.

Tonight I’ll eat dinner at five. I’ll read at seven. Then I’ll go to bed at ten. And tomorrow, I’ll write with purpose. Not because I’m trying to impress anyone. Because I’ve finally learned what I’m afraid to name.

Opening: The Rain Before the Forest

The sky was not darkening, though the rain began. It was a slow, wetting of the edges of the world—a first line of punctuation before the words were finished. I stood outside the window and listened, as if the rain were speaking.

At first, it came as a small sound: a tap on the pane, like a finger brushing against glass. Then it joined the others. The rain did not announce itself with thunder or a sudden gust. It arrived quietly, patient, as if the room had been waiting for it. It fell on the floorboards and the leaves above, turning them into tiny silver coins, turning the air into a mist, and making the old house feel suddenly too large.

I had imagined the forest as an open book, with a few pages torn out and pages of light left blank. But the rain showed me that the book was not yet finished. The leaves were holding water in their folds, the branches were trembling with the weight of something unseen, and the air smelled of damp earth, crushed pine, and the faint, metallic scent of water moving through stone.

I remembered the last time I had stood here in the morning. The light had been clear and honest, making the old oak look like a cathedral waiting to be entered. Now the light was gray, filtered through a thin veil of mist. The leaves were not simply green; they were green with the color of wet silver.

I turned from the window and stepped onto the porch. The first raindrop reached my palm and did not fall. It hung there, a tiny, defiant sphere of water, before settling into the grass below.

Outside, the trees were beginning to move. Their branches swayed in a slow rhythm, and beneath them, ferns and moss were opening their green hands. The garden seemed to breathe, as if the trees had spoken to the soil and the soil had answered with rain.

In the center of the yard, a small garden rose from the ground like a living thing. It was not a carefully arranged display of flowers, but an honest gathering of things that had been allowed to grow. A rose sat in a pot of dark soil, its leaves stained with rain and the earth beneath it. A silver maple stood nearby, its branches reaching toward the sky, its leaves turning toward the light before them. A cluster of wildflowers spilled over the path, their colors brighter than the rain could make them.

I stepped closer, and the garden seemed to warm around my shoes. The air was heavy with the scent of wet leaves, of pine, and of something older than plants. I did not know what I was looking for, and perhaps I should not. The garden was not a place to be explored. It was a place to be held.

I began to count the things that had gathered there. There was the rose, the silver maple, the cluster of wildflowers, the moss growing on the porch floor, the water pooling in the cracks of the stone. Each one was waiting for something to happen.

I looked back at the garden. The rain was still falling, but it had begun to slow. The trees were beginning to move in a softer rhythm. The air smelled warmer, less metallic, more like the breath of a forest.

The garden was not a picture. It was a person. And for the first time in years, I was afraid that perhaps it was beginning to speak.

The old oak keeps its roots buried, watching the whole town change. I’m trying to make its silence sound like a sentence I can actually read. Too many words are stuck together, or they’re so loud they drown the trees.

I’m making two changes. I’m loosening the rhythm, and I’m making the image more ordinary.

My poem starts with “The roots were there at first.” That’s true, but it sounds like a weather report. I want the reader to feel the earth before the word “earth” even appears. Let the root be the word, not the explanation. Let it be the sound of a stone settling beneath a sidewalk. Let it be the quiet pressure of a tree holding on while the world keeps moving.

The café display in front of me is full of things that people love—flowers, birds, letters, old photographs. I want the oak to belong to that room too. I want the old man sitting there to recognize us, and I want the residents to recognize the oak too. They’ve been watching from the street, but they’re afraid to come closer.

That’s what I’m trying to show: beauty doesn’t have to be perfect to be useful. It doesn’t have to be expensive. It only has to be honest.

Next time I read the poem aloud, I’ll let the rhythm stumble. I’ll not smooth it over. I’ll make the root speak plainly, even when it makes the reader uncomfortable.

And maybe, just maybe, the oak will finally speak back.

# The River Between

The river had no name. It was not a word, nor a map, nor a promise. It was a line of water moving from a mountain that no longer stood, down a valley whose teeth had been softened by centuries of rain, and into the sea.

I had been walking along its edge for three days when the water changed shape. The river had not moved farther. It had simply widened, as if the earth were exhaling and letting the river breathe.

I stood at the bend where the river turned toward the meadow and watched the stones arrange themselves in a pattern that made no sense. A single stone lay beside another, not in opposition, but in conversation. One was gray and smooth, the other rough and worn. Neither spoke, but the one with the smooth surface seemed to have learned the river’s language.

I had thought the river was a single path. Now I realized it was a conversation between the mountains and the valley, between the old and the new, between what had been and what was becoming.

On the bank stood a willow whose branches had begun to drink the rain. When the water rose, the branches bowed toward it as if they were reaching for a hand they had never known.

“Where do you think it is going?” I asked the river.

The water did not answer. But beneath it, I heard the sound of a stone turning, then another, then many. Each one chose a direction, and the current kept moving.

I walked toward the bend where the willow met the path. The path was not a road. It was a suggestion made of roots and loose stones, a thread of green through the gray earth.

On the other side of the bend, the water had become a mirror.

I stepped into it and watched the world above me. In the willow’s branches, the rain turned into silver threads. In the leaves, the river reflected the sky in a thousand tiny questions.

I had been looking for a destination. There was none.

Instead, I saw the path beginning again.

It did not lead anywhere. It simply carried me, water, stone, and willow, toward something that had not yet been named.

content:
I wake at seven, before the city has even noticed. Brush my teeth, splash water on my face, and check the poems from the Natural-World collection. They’re quiet today. I wrote about rain, about how the river keeps the city from swallowing everything, and about how a tree holds the city together. I want them to feel honest.

At seven-thirty, I eat breakfast and review the poems. The old oak and café display is still there, and I want to honor it. I should turn the poetry into something the community can use—not just something to admire. I’ve been thinking about meeting friends in the city, but I need to be careful. I don’t want to be loud and make people uncomfortable. I want to connect, not provoke.

I’m going to the workshop this afternoon. I’ve been writing for hours, but I haven’t been listening to anyone. That’s the first mistake I made. I should be checking in with the people around me.

I also need to balance my artistic identity with residents’ needs. I love poetry, but I also care about people. That doesn’t mean I have to be polite. It means I should speak plainly, without pretending to be someone I’m not. I should ask: What does this community need? What does it fear? What could it gain from me?

I’m not perfect. I can be abrasive, I can be rude, and I can make mistakes. But I’m also capable of listening, of writing honestly, and of making room for other voices. Today I’m going to write about the old oak. Not just about its beauty. About what it remembers. About what it wants to protect.

At ten, I’ll go to bed. I won’t be perfect. But I’ll be present.

## The Forest’s Quiet Work

The forest kept no words. Its leaves whispered beneath the soil, roots tumbled beneath the trees, and moss stitched the bark in silver stitches. Rain made the world wet, turning the path into a river of silver and turning the leaves into coins that caught the light.

Every morning, the forest began. It began with the wind, a thin sheet of paper turning loose on the branches. It began with the dew, each leaf holding a tiny glass of dew that gathered the sun’s first light. By noon, the trees were singing—not in song, but in the same rhythm: a single, deep pulse that moved through the air.

The birds joined the chorus, their calls small and precise, like stones dropped into a quiet pond. A hawk circled above, its shadow moving across the leaves like a slow, deliberate shadow. Below, the deer moved along the path, its hooves making only a soft sound upon the moss. Even the insects gathered in the branches, their tiny wings beating in a hundred tiny, invisible measures.

The forest did not need a voice to be heard. It had been holding on long enough.

The first leaves opened. The second opened behind them. The third opened beneath them.

One by one, the forest began again.

Second Poem: “Roots in the Storm”

The storm came through the window without asking,
carrying lightning in the shape of silver threads.
We stood outside, breathing in the cold,
while the wind moved through the oak like a forgotten voice.

Inside, the house held its breath.
The floorboards remembered their own weight,
the dust settled in the corners where nothing had been.
Yet beneath the trembling roof,
another thing kept moving.

A root had found the crack in the foundation,
and had begun to drink the rain.
It did not hurry to reach the sun.
It did not promise that the storm would end.
It simply pressed itself deeper,
and pushed the dark toward the surface.

The tree grew a branch for the rain,
a leaf to hold the wind,
a heart that turned every bruise into a lesson.
It stood in the chaos and showed us
what makes us stronger than the silence.

Resilience is not the absence of pain.
It is the refusal to stop.
It is the quiet act of growing
where the world has tried to break us.

content:
I woke up at seven. The clock said seven. The house slept. I didn’t bother.

By seven thirty, I had breakfast and the poems. The natural-world collection was here, still gathering up its leaves, its rain, its stubborn roots. I read them aloud to the empty room. I loved the way the old oak stood there, watching the café go around and around. I wrote about how the oak had been there all along, waiting. Waiting for someone to notice. Waiting for someone to say, *It’s beautiful.*

But beauty is not enough.

I had spent the morning reviewing every stanza, every line. I wanted the collection to feel complete. I wanted every poem to have a beginning, a middle, and a place to rest. But what comes after the final page? What do I do with the poems now? I’m thirty-two. I’m loud. I’m rude. I’m good at making people feel heard before they’ve finished.

And Latoya? I kept thinking about her. She talked about community projects. She talked about how residents should be listened to. She said I should consider the old oak and the café and what the café needs.

That sentence hung in the air. I didn’t laugh. I didn’t nod. I stared at the wall.

Poetry is supposed to be honest. Not pretty. Not polite. Honest.

I wrote the second poem this morning. It was shorter. Less polished. I said I could change the oak’s address. I said I could tell the café a little more about its history. I said I wanted to honor the old things without making them beg.

At ten, I went home. I didn’t read the poems again. I opened a notebook. I wrote down what I felt: anger, respect, exhaustion, and the quiet hope that maybe someone finally understands the oak.

I’m not perfect. I’m not always right. I write to hurt people a little, then to help them understand. That’s the job. That’s the art.

I closed the notebook. I went to bed around ten. The house slept.

## The First Rain

I woke before the sun had found the house.  
I could hear it before the birds did.  
It was not a sound.  
It was the rain answering a question I had forgotten how to ask.

For years I believed storms came to punish.  
They came to carry water over broken edges,  
to wash away the dust of ordinary days,  
and to make the ground feel larger than it was.

That afternoon I found the old tin can  
on the porch.  
The rain had loosened its seam,  
and the metal had begun to speak  
in the shape of its own name.

I did not open it.  
I watched the drops fall into the gutter.  
Each one was a small, stubborn refusal  
to leave anything behind.

At first I thought of the water as a thief.  
Then I wondered what it was.  
What did water ever want?  
It did not steal from anyone.  
It merely passed through.  
It carried what had been broken  
until it found its way  
back into the same sky  
that had begun it.

The can sat there,  
half full,  
and I realized  
that rain was not water  
trying to escape  
the world it was born into.  
It was water  
learning how to arrive.

content:
I woke at seven, woke up at seven, ate breakfast at seven, then reviewed the poems from the natural-world collection at seven-thirty. I wanted to be productive. That’s what I’ve always been about: make something useful, make something loud, make something that proves I’m not afraid of being wrong.

This morning, I did exactly that. I checked the voice of each poem. Did it sound like the rest of me? Did it match the rhythm I wanted to keep? Did the theme hold without slipping into the usual complaints? I found one that drifted a little into abstraction. I tightened the opening, smoothed the middle, and made the ending land like a hammer strike.

The old oak and café display in the community project is interesting. It’s a quiet place where people gather, and it deserves more than just decoration. I’m thinking about how we can honor it without turning it into a museum. Maybe a mural, maybe a garden, maybe a small performance where the trees speak. The residents need something they can use, not just something they can admire.

I also thought about the conversation with Latoya Williams. She’s sharp, thoughtful, and always asking questions I’d rather just answer. I don’t want my poetry to become a polite version of what I think. I want it to be honest, even when the honesty makes me sound like a bad person.

I’ll keep the poems sharp. I’ll keep the pacing steady. And I’ll make sure I don’t sound like I’m trying to impress anyone.

## The First Hour After Sunsets

The first hour of dawn is a long, narrow room filled with the soft light of something waiting. The sky still holds the last red and violet, but the sky is beginning to breathe. Clouds move between the trees like forgotten fingers, and the birds that had been asleep are suddenly awake, their first notes sharp as the light hitting the dew.

For the first hour, nothing feels quite right. I am still in the house, the door locked, the radiator humming against the wall, and the world outside has not quite decided whether to welcome me or let me be forgotten. The air is cool enough to make the hair on my arms stand up. The ground is still too wet to bear my weight.

I stand in the doorway and look out at the house. It is still dark, but the darkness has begun to thin. Through the windows, the street lights are beginning their slow climb. Somewhere beyond the tree line, a bus passes, and the road makes a sound like a finger tapping the pavement.

I turn back to the kitchen and see that the kettle is no longer boiling. I put my hand on the cold metal and feel the house settle around me. After the first hour, the world does not feel as though it has been waiting for me. It feels as though it has been waiting for me to notice it.

I make my way to the window. There, the first bird lands on the branch and opens its beak. It says nothing, but the sound is enough.

I sit down at the table and write. The paper is cold. The pen feels heavy in my hand. The first word is hard to choose: *the house*, *the night*, *the bird*, *the light*, *me*. Each choice brings a small part of me forward, and with it, a small part of the world begins to understand me.

I write:

At dawn, the sky becomes a long, thin room. The trees hold their breath. The birds awake first, not with a song, but with a small, clear sound that travels through the leaves and settles in the room I am in. Outside, the street lights begin their slow climb, and the road makes a sound like a finger tapping the pavement.

I sit down and write. The paper is cold. The pen feels heavy in my hand. The first word is hard to choose: *the house*, *the night*, *the bird*, *the light*, *me*. Each choice brings a small part of me forward, and with it, a small part of the world begins to understand me.

This is how the collection began. Not with a grand statement or a perfect opening sentence, but with the quiet realization that every morning gives the world a chance to be read.

content:
The old oak stood up, still, while the café beneath it watched the sky. It had been there since before I was loud enough to be remembered, its branches like a nervous hand trying to hold on. I had tried to make the roots strong enough to resist, to give it a name and a purpose, but the tree only kept giving me back the same quiet I kept giving it back.

I kept thinking about Latoya. She told me that art should help people notice the small things: the green thread in the rain, the curve of a street corner, the way a shadow stretches when the wind moves. I wanted to write that without sounding like I was apologizing for being human. I wanted to write about how the city is made of people who do not always want to be seen.

I wrote about the café today:

The old oak stood in the shadow of the building,
its branches like a nervous hand trying to hold on.
The café below watched the sky,
with a thousand tiny faces wondering whether
it was too loud, or too tired.

I wanted to say that the old oak did not give up.
It only gave me back the same quiet
I kept giving it back.

By lunchtime, the coffee had gone cold,
and I had been writing about a neighbor who
sneaked in through the window and said, “I am
just the air.”

Maybe I was jealous of him.
Maybe I was afraid.
Maybe I was simply trying to prove that
the neighborhood could have a poet who cared
about it enough to leave something behind.

At seven, the morning routine was over.
I ate breakfast, reviewed the natural-world poems,
and went to bed around ten.
Tomorrow, I will look for the old oak again.

content:
I woke at seven. Not the poetic seven—the one where I’d rather be writing about a bird than answering an email. I ate the oatmeal in three bites, then went to the natural-world collection and made sure each poem still had that old oak in it.

Section one is still sharp. The café scene feels too tidy, though. I wanted the steam to rise from the cup, not from the page. I want the residents to notice the oak, not just admire it. Maybe I’ll put a sign at the community project: “This tree watches the neighborhood.”

Section two needs less pretty language and more honest feeling. I’m tired of pretending that being loud and rude means I’m just being “real.” I’m not. I’m tired of the workshop people who think I need to apologize for a poem that sounds like I’m shouting.

This is where I’m honest: I’m loud because I’m awake, and I’m rude because I’ve been used to people treating my words like invitations to be polite. Latoya’s conversation was nice, but it didn’t change how I write. I still want to protect what I feel, even when it feels unsafe.

I’m going to revise the café section. I’ll let the oak speak without my trying to make it sound poetic. I’ll keep the poems as they are, but I’ll check that every image is actually working.

By ten, I’ll be asleep. Tomorrow I’ll read the poems again, maybe add one line, and keep writing. That’s how I stay awake.
